items.title: Taylor's piece rate was an incentive, not a wage
items.claim: F.W. Taylor at Bethlehem Steel in the 1890s introduced piece-rate pay. What was the central design feature?

options.text: All workers received the same base pay regardless of output
Workers were paid per unit produced, with the 'scientific' target set so only those following Taylor's prescribed method could earn the bonus
Piece rates were determined by union negotiation

items.reveal_title: Pay per piece, conditional on method
items.reveal:
Taylor's pig-iron handling experiments at Bethlehem Steel (1898-99) raised loading from 12.5 to 47 tons per worker per day. Workers earning the bonus received about 60% more pay; the firm got 280% more output per worker.

Unions opposed Taylorism fiercely — 1911 US Congressional hearings investigated 'speed-up' abuses. Modern piece rates persist in garment factories, gig economy (Uber surge pricing as a variant) and sales commissions.
items.why: Piece rates align effort with output but can erode quality, safety and worker autonomy. The same design principle reappears in 'pay for performance' compensation a century later.

items.title: Ford's $5 day was a retention crisis fix, not generosity
items.claim: In January 1914, Henry Ford doubled the basic wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day. What problem was he solving?

options.text: Falling demand for the Model T
Catastrophic worker turnover — the assembly line was so monotonous that annual turnover had reached around 370%, meaning the plant had to hire roughly 50,000 people to maintain a workforce of 14,000
A unionisation drive he wanted to prevent

items.reveal:
Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers's 1987 paper analysed Ford's wage decision. Turnover collapsed after the announcement; absenteeism dropped from 10% to 2.5%; productivity rose. The wage was conditional — there was a 'Sociological Department' that inspected workers' homes for 'good moral character' to qualify.

The popular story (Ford paid workers enough to buy his cars) is a post-hoc rationalisation. A Model T cost roughly $440; a workforce of 14,000 buying cars wouldn't move the market.

The wage was efficient: Ford gained productivity worth more than the extra wage bill.
items.why: Famous 'visionary' business decisions usually have boring, specific operational drivers. The $5 day looks like generosity; it was wage-efficiency arbitrage.

items.title: Ansoff said diversification was the riskiest growth strategy
items.claim: Igor Ansoff's 1957 'Strategies for Diversification' in Harvard Business Review introduced a 2x2 matrix. Which growth strategy did he flag as carrying highest risk?

options.text: Diversification (new product, new market) — combining product and market uncertainty multiplies risk

items.reveal:
Ansoff's matrix sequences risk: market penetration (existing product, existing market) is safest; product development and market development each add one source of uncertainty; diversification adds two.

Empirical work (Markides 1995, McKinsey 2010s) has supported this in aggregate: unrelated diversification destroys shareholder value more often than not. The 1960s conglomerate boom (ITT, Hanson) and its 1990s breakup vindicated Ansoff's warning.
items.why: Growth strategies look attractive on the upside; Ansoff's matrix forces you to articulate the downside risks for each route.
